item.title: Dogged by suspicions of Chinese espionage, Jensen Huang steps down as Nvidia’s boss
item.category: Nvidia and the China spying claims
item.description:
The co-founder of the AI-chip giant resigned on Thursday, after revelations of an affair with a woman whom American officials suspect of spying for Beijing. The chief financial officer, Colette Kress, takes over in the interim.

On Thursday 12 November Nvidia announced the resignation “effective immediately” of its chief executive and co-founder, Jensen Huang, 63, who also leaves the board, gave no official reason and named its chief financial officer, Colette Kress, as interim boss, Al Jazeera and The National report. On 8 November he had admitted an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singaporean firm, whom American officials suspect of spying for Beijing, while Nvidia, which controls about 90% of the market for advanced AI chips, sits at the heart of the Sino-American technology rivalry. The shares fell by more than 14% at one point on Thursday, the board, now chaired by Harvey Jones, is looking for a successor, and Republican lawmakers are threatening a subpoena to question Mr Huang about the affair’s implications for national security.

item.title: Nvidia investigates its boss, Jensen Huang, over ties to a woman suspected of spying for Beijing
item.category: Nvidia and the China spying claims
item.description:
The board of the AI-chip giant has handed an inquiry to independent directors after its chief executive’s admission. Three House committee chairmen want to question him behind closed doors.

On Sunday 8 November Nvidia’s board announced an investigation by a committee of independent directors, assisted by outside lawyers, after its chief executive, Jensen Huang, admitted an intimate relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data-centre company. According to the New York Times, American intelligence concluded that she was passing information to Beijing, which China dismisses as baseless speculation, and a Malaysian company linked to Megaspeed bought at least $4.8bn of equipment built on Nvidia technology. The board says it has no reason to believe that national security or confidential information was compromised and retains confidence in its boss, whom three House committee chairmen want to question in a closed-door session on 18 November.
